newsitem.title: UK: Seventy-two hours left to save Britain, Major says.
newsitem.headline: Seventy-two hours left to save Britain, Major says.

text.p: Prime Minister John Major wrapped up a whirlwind nationwide tour on Monday with a plea to voters to save Britain from break-up by keeping faith with his Conservative Party in Thursday's election.

With all the signs pointing to a thumping victory for Tony Blair's new-look Labour Party, Major visited Northern Ireland, Scotland and Wales to show his concern that a Blair government could bring about the dismantling of the United Kingdom.

"The message that I would give to the British nation is quite clear: you have 72 hours in which to save the Union, 72 hours to make sure that the system of government that has prevailed in this country for a very long time is protected and enshrined...not broken up and divided," Major told about 300 Conservative supporters gathered near parliament.
The latest poll released on Monday gave Labour a 19-point lead, barely changed from March 17 when Major announced a six-week election campaign -- the longest for 80 years.
But Blair warned his party it must not take for granted the victory for which it has been waiting since Margaret Thatcher ushered in 18 unbroken years of Conservative rule in 1979.
"This election is not over until it is over. The only poll that counts is the election. I don't think this is a landslide country," he told reporters in Nottingham, central England.

Aides said he later penned a message to senior colleagues who may join his cabinet on Friday reminding them Labour needs a 4.3 percent swing for outright victory, greater than any it has achieved since 1945.

Major, who was in a doggedly optimistic mood during his symbolic visit to the four corners of the country, also recalled that opinion polls failed to predict his victory in 1992 when he came from behind to secure a 21-seat majority.
"I don't believe the opinion polls. They bear no relationship to what we're finding on the doorstep," he said.
Still, if the polls are right, Labour could win the biggest majority in its history. Electoral expert Peter Kellner said he expected a 121-seat majority in the 659-member House of Commons.

Blair, who has dragged his party to the centre ground of politics since he became leader in 1994, jettisoning traditional tax-and-spend policies, is benefiting from deep divisions within the Conservatives, notably over Europe.
More than 200 Conservative candidates have openly opposed Major's wait-and-see stance on whether to join the European Union's planned single currency.
Still, Major believes talking tough on Europe can win him votes and he again hit out at what he said was Blair's willingness to transfer more power to Brussels from Britain.
"I very much favour us cooperating with our European partners. But I believe we do have to draw a line in the sand as to how far we move towards an integrated Europe," he said.

The optimism of pro-Conservative papers that rejoiced when a poll last week put the ruling party just five points adrift has given way to feverish speculation over who will succeed Major as party leader if defeat prompts him to step down.
"Tories battle to halt election wipeout," said the Daily Mail. "Major's last bid to avert disaster," said the Express.

Major's Northern Ireland visit, amid heavy security, underlined his determination not to allow the Irish Republican Army to disrupt polling day, despite recent bomb warnings that have brought chaos to British motorways and railways.

Blair accused the ruling party of "weakness, division and drift" and claimed that if it won a fifth consecutive term of office, Britain's National Health Service would be next in line for privatisation.

Blair will reinforce his no-complacency message on Tuesday with a visit to Gloucester, a marginal seat which Labour calculates it would win in an evenly-spread national swing big enough to give the party an overall parliamentary majority.
